1.pericope_label: If there arise among you a prophet, or a dreamer of dreams, and giveth thee a sign or a wonder, And the sign or the wonder come to pass, whereof he spake unto thee, saying, Let us go after other gods, which thou hast not known, and let us serve them; Thou shalt not hearken unto the words of that prophet, or that dreamer of dreams: for the Lord your God proveth you, to know whether ye love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul.

schools.summary: Set out the chapter's architecture first: three cases of instigation to idolatry are considered, the false prophet, the private individual and the city, and in every case the penalty is the same, death without mercy. Meet the suggestion that so severe a law must be the production of a later age, granting that it may have been more often broken than observed but pointing to episodes in the history which seem to require some such law in all three of its sections, since the case of the false prophet is what justifies Elijah in taking the prophets of Baal down to the brook Kishon. Then draw from the trial clause the conclusion that matters most: however great the importance attached to signs and wonders, they were not to be regarded in Israel as the highest test or as absolutely decisive, since there was a certainty there which was more certain still.

Explain why the warning comes at this point. Having restrained them from the delusions of the surrounding nations, the lawgiver now guards against false teachers arising from among themselves, since peril is to be feared not only from professed enemies but because Satan plots by intestine deceits and abuses the holy name of God to betray us; hence the faith of the godly must not only be fortified externally by the ramparts of the word against corruption creeping in from without, but garrisoned within by the same word lest novel imaginations secretly insinuate themselves. Then take up the question of divine knowledge raised by the trial clause. The verb, when applied to God, is never used in a bad sense of taking by guile or laying snares for the unwary, but only of proving or examining; God proves men's hearts not that he may learn what was before unknown but to lay open what was concealed, so that the expression to know refers to experimental knowledge only. Quote Augustine's version of the point — that God permits us to be tempted not that he may know but that he may cause us to know how far we have advanced in his love — and call it tame and involved, since human feelings are so commonly attributed to God that there is no use twisting words which signify no more than that God makes trial. Add the means by which the wonder may be done: sleight of hand, magic art, or the help of the devil, permitted for the trial of the faith of God's people.

Find the supposition strange twice over. It is strange that any should arise from among themselves, and especially any pretending to vision and prophecy, who should instigate them to serve other gods, since it seems hardly possible that a man with knowledge enough to personate a prophet should have so little knowledge of the divine nature as to go after other gods himself — and yet we see it in our own day, multitudes professing both learning and religion while exciting others to worship God by images and to give divine honour to saints and angels, such is the power of strong delusions. Stranger still is that the sign given to confirm the false doctrine should actually come to pass.

List what the two words for sign and wonder may cover, from an apparently miraculous proof of mission to a type or representation of the thing the prophet wants his hearers brought over to, and instance the images pretended to have fallen from heaven which gave rise to the Palladium and to Numa's shields. Then make experience the safeguard: God permits such impostors to arise to try the faith of his followers and put their religious experience to the test, for one who knows God experimentally cannot be drawn away after idols, whereas he who has no experimental knowledge may believe anything.

debates.question: How can the false prophet's sign actually come to pass?

sides.position: By sleight of hand, magic art, or the help of the devil, permitted for the trial of God's people and the hardening of others
God permits such impostors to arise to try the faith of his followers and put their religious experience to the test
It is the strangest part of the supposition, and shows the power of strong delusions

debates.question: What does it mean that the Lord proveth you?

sides.position: God proves men's hearts not to learn what was unknown but to lay open what was concealed; to know refers to experimental knowledge only
Augustine's version — that he permits temptation to make us know how far we have advanced — is tame and involved
However great the importance attached to signs and wonders, they were not the highest test in Israel nor absolutely decisive

debates.question: Is a law this severe credible as early legislation?

sides.position: Yes: it may have been more often broken than observed, but episodes in the history require some such law in all three of its sections
The warning was needed because peril comes not only from professed enemies but from intestine deceits under the holy name of God

outliers.note: Alone quotes Augustine’s explanation of how God can be said to learn by testing and then rejects it by name as tame and involved, preferring to treat the language as an ordinary attribution of human feeling to God.

Alone turns the strangeness of the supposition on his own century, observing that multitudes professing both learning and religion excite others to worship God by images and give divine honour to saints and angels.

themes: if there arise among you a prophet, or a dreamer of dreams
the sign or the wonder come to pass
the LORD your God proveth you

4.pericope_label: Ye shall walk after the Lord your God, and fear him, and keep his commandments, and obey his voice, and ye shall serve him, and cleave unto him. And that prophet, or that dreamer of dreams, shall be put to death; because he hath spoken to turn you away from the Lord your God, which brought you out of the land of Egypt, and redeemed you out of the house of bondage, to thrust thee out of the way which the Lord thy God commanded thee to walk in. So shalt thou put the evil away from the midst of thee.

schools.summary: Explain why the sentence follows where it does: having already warned them not to listen to all teachers indifferently but to distinguish true from false and give credit only after judgement, the lawgiver now adds the punishment of those who creep in under the name of a prophet to draw the people into rebellion. Then limit the severity twice before defending it. Do not condemn to capital punishment those who may have spread false doctrine on account of some particular or trifling error, but only those who are the authors of apostasy and pluck up religion by the roots; and hold that the season of such severity would not arrive until a positive religion had been established, since the crime of impiety would not otherwise merit punishment unless the religion had been received by public consent and were supported besides by sure and indisputable proofs. Draw the two-edged conclusion: the severity of those who defend superstitions with the sword is preposterous, yet in a well constituted polity profane men by whom religion is subverted are by no means to be tolerated. Then argue from the lesser offence to the greater — in minor offences the judge may not hesitate, yet when the worship of God is violated shall so great a crime be fostered by his dissimulation; capital punishment is decreed against adulterers, yet shall the despisers of God adulterate the doctrines of salvation with impunity; pardon is never extended to poisoners, by whom the body alone is harmed. Note also that all excuse was obviated here, since it was manifest who God is both by the blessing of the redemption from Egypt and by the doctrine of the law. Add from the Targum that the death intended was by the sword, and take the walking after the Lord as covering moral conduct, civil conduct and worship alike.

Fix who is being commanded: the execution of seducers to idolatry is enjoined upon the people, that is upon the whole community and not upon single individuals, but specifically upon the authorities who had to maintain and administer justice. Render the verb as to force thee from the way in which the Lord has commanded thee to walk, and note that the neuter in the closing formula about putting the evil away is settled by comparison with a later chapter.
Read the verb as marking the great force and power of seducers to corrupt men's minds, and gloss the closing formula tersely: thou shalt remove the guilt by removing the guilty.

debates.question: Who is commanded to carry out the sentence?

sides.position: The whole community, not single individuals, but specifically the authorities who had to maintain and administer justice
The death was by the sword, according to the Targum

debates.question: How far does the severity extend?

sides.position: Not to those who spread false doctrine through some particular or trifling error, but only to authors of apostasy who pluck up religion by the roots
And not at all until a positive religion is established by public consent and supported by indisputable proofs

debates.question: What is the closing formula about putting away evil?

sides.position: Thou shalt remove the guilt by removing the guilty
The word for evil is neuter, as comparison with a later chapter shows

outliers.note: Alone mounts an argument from lesser offences to greater in defence of the death penalty for apostasy — adulterers, poisoners, thieves — and his editor appends a long footnote treating the principle as Calvin’s final apology for his part in the death of Servetus, with a modern historian’s four points in his defence.
Alone fixes the addressee of the command, distinguishing the whole community from single individuals and locating the duty specifically in the authorities charged with administering justice.

themes: ye shall walk after the LORD your God
that prophet shall be put to death
so shalt thou put the evil away from the midst of thee

6.pericope_label: If thy brother, the son of thy mother, or thy son, or thy daughter, or the wife of thy bosom, or thy friend, which is as thine own soul, entice thee secretly, saying, Let us go and serve other gods, which thou hast not known, thou, nor thy fathers; Namely, of the gods of the people which are round about you, nigh unto thee, or far off from thee, from the one end of the earth even unto the other end of the earth; Thou shalt not consent unto him, nor hearken unto him; neither shall thine eye pity him, neither shalt thou spare, neither shalt thou conceal him: But thou shalt surely kill him; thine hand shall be first upon him to put him to death, and afterwards the hand of all the people. And thou shalt stone him with stones, that he die; because he hath sought to thrust thee away from the Lord thy God, which brought thee out of the land of Egypt, from the house of bondage. And all Israel shall hear, and fear, and shall do no more any such wickedness as this is among you.

schools.summary: Take the phrase about the son of thy mother not as marking a half-brother but as bringing out the closeness of the fraternal relation, matching it with the wife of thy bosom who rests upon thy breast and the friend who is as thine own soul, meaning one loved as much as life itself. Find a safeguard in the requirement that the witness strike first, since where a witness must himself carry out or help carry out the sentence he demands, secret accusation becomes impossible and it is far less easy to pervert the law to prosecute a private quarrel. Then guard the closing clause about all Israel hearing and fearing: the fear of punishment given here as the end of the punishment is not the principle lying at the foundation of the law, but simply, as Calvin expresses it, the utility and fruit of severity, one reason for carrying it out and not to be confounded with the deterrent theory. Trace the law's later operation, holding that it justifies Jehu and Jehoiada in destroying Baal and accounts for the covenant made under Asa; and add that though it may seem harsh its principle reappears in the gospel sayings about loving father or mother more than Christ.

Explain why the same penalty reaches a private person: although his ignorance is more excusable and no office increases his responsibility, apostasy is intolerable to God from whatever quarter it arises — while keeping the two limits already laid down, that this judgment can have no place except where religion is duly constituted, and that the severity is for apostates only and not for those who have erred in some particular. Insist that vengeance was not to be executed privately without a public trial, and explain the custom of the witnesses throwing the first stone as an admirable provision, that those who denounced the crime should be the executors of its punishment in order to be more cautious and moderate in giving their testimony. Then hear in the reason annexed an aggravation drawn from ingratitude, since it was gross wickedness to rebel against God after knowing him but grosser still to undervalue the Deliverer. Supply also the evidentiary machinery: the offender was not to be killed where the enticement happened nor by the enticed on his own authority, but after sentence by the great council at Jerusalem — and since the affair was secret, report the rabbinic answer that they laid wait for the enticer, the enticed setting two witnesses behind a hedge where they could see and hear without being seen, and then asking him to repeat privately what he had said.

Read the list of relations as a study in the tempter's method. It is his policy to send his solicitations by the hand of those we love, whom we least suspect of a bad design and are most desirous to please, so that the enticement comes from a brother or child near by nature and a wife or friend near by choice; instance the tempting of Adam by Eve and of Christ by Peter, and draw the caution that we must guard against a bad proposal precisely when the person making it can plead an interest in us, that we may never sin against God in compliment to the best friend we have. Note too that the temptation is supposed to be private, which implies that idolatry is a work of darkness dreading the light and coveting to be concealed.

debates.question: Why are the nearest relations named?

sides.position: Because it is the tempter's policy to send solicitations by the hand of those we love and least suspect
To bring out the closeness of the relation — the wife of thy bosom, the friend who is as thine own soul
Because a private individual's enticement is a lighter offence and yet apostasy is intolerable to God from whatever quarter

debates.question: How could a secret enticement ever be proved?

sides.position: By the rabbinic device of laying wait: two witnesses set behind a hedge to hear the enticer repeat himself
The requirement that the witness strike first prevents false accusation, since secret accusation then becomes impossible

debates.question: Is fear of punishment the principle of the law?

sides.position: No: it is the utility and fruit of severity, one reason for carrying the law out, not to be confounded with the deterrent theory
The death of one is a wholesome discipline for all in the way of example

outliers.note: Alone confronts the evidentiary problem of a secret enticement and reports the rabbinic device for meeting it, that witnesses were set behind a hedge to overhear the enticer repeat himself — a stratagem used, they say, for no other offender.

Alone quotes Calvin by name in order to borrow his phrase and then guard it, accepting fear of punishment as the utility and fruit of severity while denying that it is the principle of the law or the deterrent theory.

themes: if thy brother entice thee secretly
thine hand shall be first upon him
all Israel shall hear, and fear

12.pericope_label: If thou shalt hear say in one of thy cities, which the Lord thy God hath given thee to dwell there, saying, Certain men, the children of Belial, are gone out from among you, and have withdrawn the inhabitants of their city, saying, Let us go and serve other gods, which ye have not known; Then shalt thou enquire, and make search, and ask diligently; and, behold, if it be truth, and the thing certain, that such abomination is wrought among you;

schools.summary: Correct the construction, since the preposition never means of one, so that the sense is not hearing in one city about another but simply hearing that in one of thy cities worthless men have risen up. Describe what the inquiry required: the people as a whole, through their rulers, were to examine closely whether the thing was founded in truth, and the phrase about all that is in it relates to men, cattle and material property alike rather than to men only. On the name given to the instigators, report that modern scholars generally explain it as worthlessness, note that this is the first place the expression occurs with a passage in Judges the second, and record that Rashi curiously makes it destroyers of the yoke. Find only one instance of the case in the history, that of Gibeah, and argue it fairly: the abominations done there may be assumed connected with idolatry from later allusions, though it was the outrage rather than the idolatry that roused Israel, and the remonstrance with the Benjamites seems to echo the language of this very chapter.

Infer the atrocity of the crime from the scale of the sentence: the severity of a just and moderate ruler in a sedition does not usually go beyond punishing the ringleaders, so that when God commands all without exception to be destroyed the great atrocity is made apparent — from which we are admonished that zeal for God's glory is but cold among us unless true religion is held of more value than the preservation of a single city or people. Set out the grammatical grounds for both readings of the name, that if the vowel points are conceded the word is compounded so as to mean one thing while if they are disregarded it may be read as insubmissive or rebellious, and then declare the second opinion the more correct, that these are men of nothing in whom nothing good or praiseworthy is found. Add the observation that gives the phrase its point, that men do not all break into impiety at the same moment but Satan stirs up some who act as fans to excite the rest. Then supply the rabbinic procedure in full: the case fell only to the great council, which inquired until it knew clearly that the whole city or the greater part was turned; two disciples of the wise were sent to admonish them, and if they repented it was well, but if they continued all Israel was ordered up against them until the city was broken up, after which courts were set up to judge the inhabitants one by one.

Mark two limits on the third case before describing it. The crime is supposed to be committed by one of the cities of Israel, lying within the jurisdiction of their own courts, since the church judged only those within; those born within a prince's allegiance who take up arms are dealt with as traitors, while foreign invaders are not. And the city supposed is one that formerly worshipped the true God and has now withdrawn to others, which shows how great the crime is and how sore the punishment of those who turn aside after they have known the way of righteousness.
Derive the name from two words meaning not and profit, cite the Greek version for lawless men, and gloss it as persons good for nothing to themselves or others and capable of nothing but mischief.

debates.question: What does the name given to the instigators mean?

sides.position: From two words meaning not and profit — good for nothing to themselves or others
Men of nothing, in whom nothing good or praiseworthy is found; the reading that makes them merely insubmissive is less correct
Worthlessness, on the general explanation of modern scholars — though Rashi curiously makes it destroyers of the yoke

debates.question: Was this case ever actually met with?

sides.position: Only at Gibeah, where the outrage rather than the idolatry roused Israel, though the remonstrance echoes this chapter's language
The city supposed is one that formerly worshipped the true God and has now withdrawn, which is what makes the crime great

debates.question: What did the commanded inquiry involve?

sides.position: Examination by the people through their rulers, whether the thing was founded in truth
A sequence reserved to the great council: inquiry, then two admonishers sent, then war, then courts judging each inhabitant on two witnesses

outliers.note: Alone searches the later history for an instance of the case and finds only Gibeah, granting candidly that it was the outrage rather than the idolatry which roused Israel.
Alone sets out the whole rabbinic procedure as a sequence of steps — inquiry, admonition by two disciples of the wise, war, siege, and then courts judging the inhabitants one by one.

themes: certain men, the children of Belial
then shalt thou inquire, and make search
withdrawn the inhabitants of their city

15.pericope_label: Thou shalt surely smite the inhabitants of that city with the edge of the sword, destroying it utterly, and all that is therein, and the cattle thereof, with the edge of the sword. And thou shalt gather all the spoil of it into the midst of the street thereof, and shalt burn with fire the city, and all the spoil thereof every whit, for the Lord thy God: and it shall be an heap for ever; it shall not be built again. And there shall cleave nought of the cursed thing to thine hand: that the Lord may turn from the fierceness of his anger, and shew thee mercy, and have compassion upon thee, and multiply thee, as he hath sworn unto thy fathers; When thou shalt hearken to the voice of the Lord thy God, to keep all his commandments which I command thee this day, to do that which is right in the eyes of the Lord thy God.

schools.summary: Explain why the promise of mercy and increase is attached to the command about the accursed thing: nothing whatever was to remain hanging to the hand of Israel, so that the Lord might turn from his wrath and have compassion on the nation — that is, not punish the sin of one town upon the whole people but multiply it, making up the diminution consequent on the destruction of that town's inhabitants and so fulfilling the promise given to the fathers. Hear an echo of the verse in the close of the story of Achan, where all Israel stoned him and raised a great heap of stones and the Lord turned from the fierceness of his anger; and match the burning of the city and the destruction of its cattle to the treatment of Gibeah.

Face the hardest form of the objection without softening it: if any should say that the little children at least were innocent, answer that since all are condemned by the judgment of God from the least to the greatest, we contend against him in vain. Give the reason for thinking the error unpardonable in the adults, that its authors were educated in the law and could not be deceived involuntarily unless they had grown weary of religion and set their hearts on the impostures of the devil; and cite Jeremiah sending the people to distant isles to ask whether any nation has changed its gods, which are yet no gods. On the burning of the spoil, distinguish two possible reasons and prefer one: it might be that the intention was to obviate covetousness lest zeal be mixed up with rapine, but the principal reason is the one the text gives, that the people might be more accustomed to detest a crime they saw so cruelly punished. Press the Hebrew word, which properly means destruction or abolition, and note that what God would have annihilated because he cannot bear the sight of it is so called before him, which is why the phrase should be rendered thou shalt burn it to the Lord thy God rather than for him. Explain what cleaving to the hand would have meant by pointing to Achan, since all being devoted to destruction was cursed and would bring a curse on whoever made it his own property; and report the rabbinic detail that if a city had no street they made one.

Restrict the word for the inhabitants to those who are guilty and not the innocent part, meaning such as disowned the apostasy, who would doubtless have left so wicked a place by their own choice or at least upon warning. Explain the completeness of the destruction by a parallel, that it is the punishment inflicted on the cities of the Canaanites, to whom having made themselves equal in sin it is just that God should equal them in punishment. Then draw a consequence from the prohibition of spoil that no one else reaches: since they were not permitted to take the spoils of these cities, they could be under no temptation to make war on them, the thing being possible only from a religious motive since no profit could come of it — and add that few religious wars would ever have been fought had they been regulated by the principle that one may neither extend territory nor take spoil. Say that the contagion had to be destroyed in its birth, that the ruin was to stand as an eternal monument and a terror to after ages, and that the people should have no loss of their numbers by cutting off so many.

debates.question: Does the sentence fall on the innocent inhabitants too?

sides.position: Only on the guilty; those who disowned the apostasy would have left the place by choice or upon warning
Even the little children: since all are condemned by the judgment of God from the least to the greatest, we contend against him in vain

debates.question: Why was the spoil to be burned rather than taken?

sides.position: Chiefly that the people might be more accustomed to detest a crime they saw so cruelly punished — though obviating covetousness may be a secondary reason
Because taking spoil would have given a motive for such wars; as it is, they could be undertaken only from a religious motive
Because whatever cleaved to the hand would bring a curse on the taker, as it did on Achan

debates.question: Why is a promise of increase attached?

sides.position: So that God might not punish the sin of one town upon the nation, but make up the diminution and fulfil the promise to the fathers
So that they should have no loss of their numbers by cutting off so many people

outliers.note: Alone restricts the sentence to the guilty and supposes the innocent would have left the city of their own choice or upon warning, against a reading that extends the destruction even to the children.

Alone draws from the prohibition of spoil a general reflection on war, that few religious wars would ever have been fought had they been regulated by the principle that one may neither extend territory nor take plunder.

themes: destroying it utterly, and all that is therein
it shall be an heap for ever
that the LORD may turn from the fierceness of his anger
